topic: S1.1 Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
subject: chemistry

items.q: Which substance is a compound, and for the correct reason?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide, since it contains atoms of two elements bonded in a fixed ratio
items.misconception: Oxygen, since each of its molecules contains two atoms bonded together
items.why: Students meet 'molecule' and 'compound' together in formulae such as H₂O and CO₂ and come to treat the two words as meaning the same thing. Confusion between molecules and compounds, and classing diatomic elements as compounds, is widely reported in research on students' ideas about elements and compounds. Ask how many different elements are present, not how many atoms. O₂ contains only oxygen atoms, so it is an element that exists as molecules. CO₂ contains carbon and oxygen atoms bonded in a fixed 1:2 ratio, so it is a compound.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.
items.random_wrong: Air, since it contains several elements in the same proportions everywhere

items.q: Hydrogen and oxygen gases are mixed and ignited. They react to form water. Which statement about the water formed is correct?
items.correct: Its hydrogen and oxygen are bonded together in a fixed ratio
items.misconception: Its hydrogen and oxygen can be separated again simply by boiling it
items.why: Students learn separation techniques and classification in the same lessons and blur the boundary between compound and mixture, which is one of the most widely reported confusions in research on students' ideas about substances. Use the test the guide gives: components that are not chemically bonded (a mixture) can be separated physically; atoms that are chemically bonded (a compound) cannot. Iron and sulfur powders can be separated with a magnet; iron(II) sulfide cannot.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.
items.random_wrong: Its hydrogen and oxygen each keep their own properties

items.q: A student dissolves sodium chloride in water to make a clear, colourless solution. Which statement about the solution is correct?
items.correct: It is a homogeneous mixture, since its composition is the same throughout the solution
items.misconception: It is a heterogeneous mixture, since the dissolved salt slowly sinks to the bottom
items.why: Students picture the dissolved solid as tiny grains that are heavier than water and so should sink, as sand does. Non-uniform ideas about solutions, with solute collecting at the bottom, are widely reported in research on students' ideas about dissolving. Dissolved particles are individual ions or molecules surrounded by solvent molecules and kept in constant random motion, so they stay uniformly distributed. Only undissolved solid, as in a heterogeneous mixture such as sand in water, settles.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.
items.random_wrong: It is a compound, since the salt and water have bonded together in solution

items.q: A mixture of sand and sodium chloride is stirred with hot water and then filtered. Where is the sodium chloride after filtration?
items.correct: In the filtrate, as ions surrounded by water molecules
items.misconception: On the filter paper, since solid cannot pass through it
items.why: Students know that filtration separates solids from liquids and apply this to any solid, without distinguishing an insoluble solid from a dissolved one. Examiner reports and research on separation techniques commonly note answers proposing filtration to remove dissolved salt. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. A dissolved solid is in the filtrate. To recover it, evaporate the solvent; to recover the solvent, distil.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.
items.random_wrong: Nowhere, since the salt stopped existing when it dissolved

items.q: A student wants to obtain pure water from aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Which method should be used?
items.correct: Distillation, as the water vapour is condensed and collected
items.misconception: Evaporation, as the water is collected when it leaves the dish
items.why: Both techniques involve heating a solution until the solvent vaporizes, and students remember the heating but not the condensing step. Examiner reports on separation techniques commonly note evaporation being given where distillation is needed. Ask which component is wanted. Solute wanted: evaporate (or crystallize) and let the solvent escape. Solvent wanted: distil, so that the vapour is condensed and collected.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.
items.random_wrong: Filtration, as the dissolved solid is caught by the paper

items.q: A spot of black ink is placed on the baseline of a strip of chromatography paper, and the bottom of the paper is dipped in water. As the water rises, the ink separates into three coloured spots at different heights. What does this show about the ink?
items.correct: It is a mixture of several different dyes
items.misconception: It is a mixture of several different elements
items.why: In everyday language 'element' means a component or ingredient ('the elements of a plan'), and students carry this meaning into chemistry. The loose use of 'element' for any component or substance is widely reported in research on students' ideas about substances. In chemistry an element is a substance that cannot be broken down chemically into simpler substances. The components of a mixture can be elements or compounds; the dyes in ink are compounds.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.
items.random_wrong: It is a compound the paper has separated out

items.q: Impure solid X is dissolved in the minimum volume of hot water, and the hot solution is filtered. When the filtrate is cooled, crystals of X form. Why do crystals of X form when the solution is cooled?
items.correct: X is less soluble in cold water than in hot water, so the excess comes out of solution
items.misconception: X freezes, as the solution is cooled below the temperature at which X melts
items.why: In both cases a solid seems to turn into a liquid, and everyday language uses 'melt' loosely for sugar in tea. Confusing dissolving with melting is one of the most widely reported findings in research on students' ideas about dissolving. Ask whether a second substance is needed. Melting needs only heat; dissolving needs a solvent. Melting gives one pure substance in the liquid state, (l); dissolving gives a solution, (aq).
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.
items.random_wrong: Dissolved X sinks and collects at the bottom of the flask as the water cools

items.q: A student wants to recover all of the potassium chloride, as a solid, from a dilute aqueous solution of potassium chloride. Which method should be used?
items.correct: Evaporation, as the water escapes and the solid is left behind
items.misconception: Filtration, as the dissolved solid is held back on the paper
items.why: Students know that filtration separates solids from liquids and apply this to any solid, without distinguishing an insoluble solid from a dissolved one. Examiner reports and research on separation techniques commonly note answers proposing filtration to remove dissolved salt. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. A dissolved solid is in the filtrate. To recover it, evaporate the solvent; to recover the solvent, distil.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.
items.random_wrong: Cooling, as the dissolved solid freezes when cold enough

items.q: A substance at room temperature has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container. Which statement about its particles is correct?
items.correct: They are close together but not in fixed positions
items.misconception: They are spaced about halfway between those of a solid and a gas
items.why: Liquids are shown as intermediate between solids and gases in many diagrams, and students interpolate the spacing as well as the freedom of movement. Drawings of liquids with widely spaced particles are widely reported in research on the particle model. A liquid is almost as incompressible as a solid and has a similar density, so its particles must be almost as close together. What changes on melting is that particles gain the freedom to move past one another.
items.specStatementText: The kinetic molecular theory is a model to explain physical properties of matter (solids, liquids and gases) and changes of state.
items.random_wrong: The spaces between the particles are filled with air

items.q: Which statement about the vaporization of water is correct?
items.correct: Evaporation takes place at the surface, even well below the boiling point
items.misconception: Evaporation can take place only once the water has reached its boiling point
items.why: Students connect 'turning into a gas' with a kettle boiling, and the boiling point is taught as 'the temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas'. Confusing evaporation with boiling is widely reported in research on students' ideas about changes of state. The particles in a liquid have a range of kinetic energies. At any temperature some particles at the surface have enough energy to overcome the attractions and escape, so puddles dry and wet washing dries well below 100 °C.
items.specStatementText: The kinetic molecular theory is a model to explain physical properties of matter (solids, liquids and gases) and changes of state.
items.random_wrong: The large bubbles in boiling water contain hydrogen and oxygen

items.q: Which change of state is correctly named and correctly represented by an equation with state symbols?
items.correct: Sublimation: CO₂(s) → CO₂(g)
items.misconception: Condensation: H₂O(g) → H₂O(s)
items.why: In everyday language 'condensation' describes any moisture or frost that forms on a cold window, and deposition is rarely named outside chemistry. Confusion over the names of changes of state is commonly noted in examiner reports. Name the change by its start and end states. Gas → liquid is condensation; gas → solid directly is deposition; solid → gas directly is sublimation.
items.specStatementText: The kinetic molecular theory is a model to explain physical properties of matter (solids, liquids and gases) and changes of state.

items.q: On a cold, clear night, water vapour in the air turns directly into ice crystals on a car windscreen, without first becoming liquid water. What is the name of this change of state?
items.correct: Deposition
items.misconception: Freezing
items.why: Everyday language calls ice on a windscreen "frozen" and uses "freeze" for anything becoming icy; students name the change by its end state only. Name a change of state by both its start and end states: liquid → solid is freezing; gas → solid is deposition.
items.specStatementText: The kinetic molecular theory is a model to explain physical properties of matter (solids, liquids and gases) and changes of state.

items.q: A molecular solid, X, is heated at a constant rate. Its temperature rises to 80 °C, stays at 80 °C for six minutes while the solid melts, and then rises again. Which explains why the temperature stays constant while X melts?
items.correct: The energy absorbed overcomes attractions between molecules; their average Ek is constant
items.misconception: The energy supplied is lost to the surroundings, so X absorbs none of it as it melts
items.why: Students learn 'heating makes particles move faster' and 'heating raises the temperature' as general rules and apply them during changes of state. The belief that temperature keeps rising during melting or boiling is widely reported in research on students' thermal concepts. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. During melting or boiling the temperature is constant, so the average kinetic energy does not change; the energy absorbed goes into separating the particles against their attractions.
items.specStatementText: The temperature, T, in Kelvin (K) is a measure of average kinetic energy Ek of particles.
items.random_wrong: The energy absorbed breaks the covalent bonds within each of the molecules of X

items.q: A sample of neon gas is at 77 °C. It is heated until the average kinetic energy of its atoms has doubled. What is its new temperature? (T/K = T/°C + 273)
items.why:
Everyday temperatures are given in °C, and students apply 'double the temperature, double the energy' to the number they know without asking where the scale's zero is. This is commonly noted in examiner reports on temperature-dependent calculations. Only a scale that starts at absolute zero, where the average kinetic energy is at its minimum, gives a temperature proportional to average kinetic energy. Convert to kelvin before scaling: 20 °C is 293 K, and doubling the average kinetic energy gives 586 K, which is 313 °C, not 40 °C.

Working: Average Ek ∝ T (in K). T₁ = 77 + 273 = 350 K. Doubling the average kinetic energy doubles T: T₂ = 2 × 350 K = 700 K. In °C: 700 − 273 = 427 °C.
items.specStatementText: The temperature, T, in Kelvin (K) is a measure of average kinetic energy Ek of particles.
items.working: Average Ek ∝ T (in K). T₁ = 77 + 273 = 350 K. Doubling the average kinetic energy doubles T: T₂ = 2 × 350 K = 700 K. In °C: 700 − 273 = 427 °C.

items.q: Which statement about temperature is correct?
items.correct: A rise of 1 K is exactly the same size as a rise of 1 °C
items.misconception: A temperature of 0 K is the same as a temperature of 273 °C
items.why: Students memorize '273' and 'add' as the conversion without the direction. Conversion-direction errors are commonly noted in examiner reports on temperature calculations. Check the answer: the number in kelvin is always 273 larger than the number in °C, so converting K to °C must make the number smaller: subtract 273.
items.specStatementText: The temperature, T, in Kelvin (K) is a measure of average kinetic energy Ek of particles.
items.random_wrong: Doubling a temperature in °C doubles the average kinetic energy

items.q: Is air a compound?
items.correct: No. Air is a mixture, mainly of nitrogen and oxygen with argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour, which are not bonded to one another and whose proportions vary (the water vapour content especially).
items.misconception: Any material that contains more than one element, such as air, is a compound; air has a fixed composition, so it must be a compound.
items.why: Air is taught with a list of percentages (about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen) that look like a fixed formula, and 'containing more than one element' is taken as the definition of a compound. Classifying air as a compound, and mixtures of elements as compounds, is widely reported in chemistry-education research. A compound has its elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. The nitrogen and oxygen in air are separate N₂ and O₂ molecules that are not bonded to each other; they keep their own properties and can be separated by a physical method (fractional distillation of liquid air). A mixture can contain several elements.

items.q: When sodium chloride dissolves in water, does it form a compound with the water?
items.correct: No. Salt water is a mixture. The Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions become surrounded by water molecules, but no new substance is formed: the ratio of salt to water can vary, and evaporating the water gives back sodium chloride.
items.misconception: When a solid dissolves, it combines with the water to form a new compound, so salt water is a compound.
items.why: The solid seems to vanish and a clear liquid with new properties (salty taste, conducts electricity) is left, which looks like a chemical change. Treating dissolving as a chemical reaction and solutions as compounds is widely reported in research on students' ideas about solutions. Dissolving is a physical process. The proportions in a solution are not fixed (a little or a lot of salt can dissolve, up to a limit), and the components are recovered unchanged by physical methods such as evaporation or distillation. Both points show a mixture, not a compound.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. items.q: Do the elements in a compound keep their own properties?
items.correct: No. A compound has its own properties, different from those of its elements. Sodium chloride is not a reactive metal and does not contain chlorine gas.
items.misconception: The elements in a compound keep their own properties, so a compound behaves like a combination of its elements.
items.why: Everyday 'mixing' language ('iron and sulfur combine') and the fact that a compound's name contains its elements' names suggest that the elements are still present in their original form. This is widely reported in research on students' ideas about compounds. In a compound the atoms are bonded, so the substance has new properties. Keeping the properties of each component is a property of a mixture: a mixture of iron and sulfur powders is still attracted to a magnet because the iron is unchanged.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.

items.q: What happens to a solid such as sodium chloride when it dissolves in water?
items.correct: Its particles separate and spread throughout the water, each surrounded by water molecules. The sodium chloride is still present, and it can be recovered by evaporating the water.
items.misconception: When a solid dissolves it disappears: it no longer exists, and only water is left.
items.why: Once dissolved, the solid can no longer be seen, and everyday language says sugar 'disappears' in tea. The idea that dissolved substances cease to exist is widely reported in research on students' ideas about dissolving. The mass of a solution equals the mass of solvent plus the mass of solute, and the solute can be recovered unchanged. The solute's particles are too small to see once they are separated and surrounded by solvent molecules.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. items.q: Does a separation technique such as chromatography produce new substances?
items.correct: No. Separation techniques are physical processes: the substances that come out were already present in the mixture, unchanged.
items.misconception: When a mixture is separated, the substances react with the solvent (or with the heat) and new substances are formed.
items.why: New colours or crystals appearing looks like a chemical change, and students who are unsure of the difference between physical and chemical changes treat any visible change as a reaction. Confusion between physical and chemical change is widely reported in chemistry-education research. The spots in chromatography are the dyes that were already mixed in the ink; the solvent and paper only spread them out. Recombining the separated components gives back the original mixture.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. items.q: Does the amount of a solid that water can dissolve depend on temperature?
items.correct: Yes. For most solids, solubility increases with temperature, so a hot solution can hold more solute than the same volume of cold solution. Cooling a saturated hot solution makes the excess solute crystallize.
items.misconception: The amount of solid that can dissolve does not depend on temperature (or there is no limit to how much can dissolve), so crystals appear only when the water evaporates.
items.why: Everyday experience shows solids dissolving faster in hot water but not that more dissolves, and saturation is rarely observed outside the laboratory. Ideas that there is no limit to dissolving, or that the limit does not change with temperature, are reported in research on students' ideas about solutions. A given volume of solvent can dissolve only a limited amount of a solute at a given temperature. Recrystallization depends on the solute being much more soluble in the hot solvent than in the cold solvent.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. items.q: What is between the particles of a substance?
items.correct: Nothing: the space between particles is empty (a vacuum).
items.misconception: There is air (or some other substance) in the spaces between the particles.
items.why: The idea of empty space is counter-intuitive: everyday experience says that 'empty' spaces contain air, so students fill the gaps in particle diagrams with air. This is one of the most widely reported findings in research on students' particle ideas. Air is itself made of particles (N₂ and O₂ molecules), so it cannot be what fills the gaps between particles. In the kinetic molecular theory the space between particles, including between the particles of air, is empty.
items.specStatementText: The kinetic molecular theory is a model to explain physical properties of matter (solids, liquids and gases) and changes of state.

items.q: Do the particles themselves expand, soften or melt when a substance is heated or melts?
items.correct: No. The particles do not change in size or shape. On heating they move more (vibrate more, or move faster), and on melting they break free of fixed positions; these changes in motion and arrangement explain expansion and changes of state.
items.misconception: Particles have the properties of the bulk substance, so they expand when heated and become soft or melt when the substance melts.
items.why: Students transfer the observable (macroscopic) properties of a substance to its particles. Attributing expansion, melting or softness to individual particles is one of the most widely reported findings in research on students' particle ideas. Properties such as melting, expansion and softness belong to the collection of particles, not to one particle. Expansion is an increase in the average distance between particles; melting is a change in their arrangement and motion.
items.specStatementText: The kinetic molecular theory is a model to explain physical properties of matter (solids, liquids and gases) and changes of state.

items.q: What are the bubbles in boiling water made of?
items.correct: Water vapour, H₂O(g). The water molecules stay intact; boiling separates the molecules from one another.
items.misconception: The bubbles in boiling water are hydrogen and oxygen gas, because boiling breaks water down into its elements.
items.why: Students know that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen and that gases form bubbles, so they conclude that boiling splits the molecules. The claim that the bubbles are hydrogen and oxygen is widely reported in research on students' ideas about boiling. Boiling is a physical change: it overcomes the attractions between water molecules, not the covalent bonds within them. Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen is a chemical change needing far more energy (for example electrolysis). Condensing the vapour gives back water.
items.specStatementText: The kinetic molecular theory is a model to explain physical properties of matter (solids, liquids and gases) and changes of state.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does (aq) mean the same as (l)?
items.correct: No. (l) means a pure substance in the liquid state, such as H₂O(l). (aq) means dissolved in water, such as NaCl(aq). Water itself is never written H₂O(aq).
items.misconception: (aq) and (l) both mean 'liquid', so they can be used for any liquid, including water itself.
items.why: Aqueous solutions are liquids and 'aq' is associated with water, so students use (aq) for water and for other liquids. Examiner reports commonly note incorrect state symbols such as H₂O(aq). Ask whether the substance is dissolved in water. If it is, (aq); if it is a pure liquid, (l). A solution of a substance in water is a mixture, so (aq) describes a component of a mixture.
items.specStatementText: The kinetic molecular theory is a model to explain physical properties of matter (solids, liquids and gases) and changes of state.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a molecular substance melts or boils, are the covalent bonds within its molecules broken?
items.correct: No. Melting and boiling overcome the attractions between molecules. The covalent bonds within the molecules are unchanged, which is why the substance is the same before and after.
items.misconception: When a molecular substance melts or boils, the covalent bonds inside its molecules break.
items.why: 'Bonds are broken' is a common phrase, and students do not distinguish the attractions between molecules from the covalent bonds within them. This is widely reported in research on students' ideas about bonding and changes of state. If covalent bonds broke on melting, the substance would change into other substances, and freezing the liquid would not give back the same solid. A change of state is a physical change: the molecules stay intact.

items.q: After converting a temperature to kelvin for a calculation, must the answer be converted back to °C if the question asks for °C?
items.correct: Yes. A result calculated in kelvin is a kelvin value; if the answer is wanted in °C, subtract 273.
items.misconception: Once a temperature has been converted to kelvin for a calculation, the number obtained can be given as the answer in °C without converting back.
items.why: Students learn to convert to kelvin at the start of temperature calculations but treat the conversion as a one-way preliminary step, so the final kelvin value is reported with the unit the question used. Answers left in kelvin when °C was asked for are commonly noted in examiner reports. Check the unit asked for at the end of every calculation: 700 K is 700 − 273 = 427 °C.
items.specStatementText: The temperature, T, in Kelvin (K) is a measure of average kinetic energy Ek of particles.

items.q: Are heat and temperature the same thing?
items.correct: No. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, measured in joules. Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles, measured in kelvin.
items.misconception: Temperature and heat are the same thing: the temperature of an object measures how much heat it contains.
items.why: Everyday language uses 'heat' for hotness ('turn up the heat'), and the two words are used in the same situations. The fusion of heat with temperature is one of the most widely reported findings of research on students' thermal concepts. Temperature does not depend on the amount of substance: a bath and a cup of water can both be at 40 °C, though the bath would transfer far more energy as heat to its surroundings as it cools. Temperature describes a state; heat describes a transfer of energy.
items.specStatementText: The temperature, T, in Kelvin (K) is a measure of average kinetic energy Ek of particles.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the composition of a compound depend on the amounts of the elements used to make it?
items.correct: No. A compound always contains its elements in the same fixed ratio. If more of one reactant is used than is needed, the excess is left over unreacted; it does not become part of the compound.
items.misconception: A compound's composition depends on how much of each element was used to make it, so using more of one element gives a compound containing more of that element.
items.why: In a mixture the proportions do follow the amounts mixed, and students carry this over to the product of a reaction. The idea that excess reactant is built into the product is reported in research on students' understanding of chemical reactions and limiting reactants. Pure water is always H₂O, whether it is made from equal volumes of hydrogen and oxygen (which leaves oxygen over) or from a 2:1 mixture. A fixed ratio of elements is exactly what distinguishes a compound from a mixture.
items.specStatementText: Elements are the primary constituents of matter, which cannot be chemically broken down into simpler substances. Compounds consist of atoms of different elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. Mixtures contain more than one element or compound in no fixed ratio, which are not chemically bonded and so can be separated by physical methods.

items.q: Is the direct change from gas to solid called sublimation?
items.correct: No. Sublimation is solid → gas; the reverse, gas → solid, is deposition.
items.misconception: Sublimation is the name for any direct change between solid and gas, in either direction.
items.why: Older texts and meteorology have used "sublimation" for vapour turning directly to ice, and the solid formed from a vapour is still called a "sublimate"; students also meet sublimation far more often than deposition. Sublimation and deposition are a reverse pair, like melting and freezing: solid → gas is sublimation; gas → solid is deposition.
